newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - Digi on track to profitability.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Digi on track to profitability.

text.p: U.S.-based computer communications firm Digi International Inc could return to profits sooner-than-expected, in the third quarter of its current fiscal year, said a senior official on Tuesday.

"We are planning to be profitable. My commitment to the board is by the end of the fiscal year but it could be sooner in Q3," Jerry Dusa, Digi's president and chief executive officer told Reuters in an interview.
Dusa said gross margins would remain in the high 40-low 50 percent region. Margins after operating expenses would be about 15 percent.
Digi provides hardware and software to connect users to computer networks, termed remote access, or to a computer, called multi-user.

For its second quarter, it reported a loss of US$9.4 million which included a US$10.5 million restructuring charge and a US$1.6 million loss for its investment in AetherWorks Corp, a development stage company.
It saw a loss of US$2.6 million in the first quarter, including a loss of US$1.5 million in AetherWorks.
Dusa said Digi's fortunes sank as expenses outstripped revenue growth.
"Expenses grew faster than our turnover while we were attempting to invest in too many businesses and too many locations, and expanding too rapidly," he said.
He said over the last five years, Digi had acquired five companies in associated businesses and found itself faced with many competitors with many different kinds of technologies.

Digi had now narrowed its product line, consolidated manufacturing and engineering and cut staff by about 20 percent. It was putting its efforts behind remote access technology, which is driven by Internet and Intranet (corporate networks with links to the internet) connections.
"It is going to cause millions of new communications ports to be installed in the next five years and our strategy is to be the dominant provider of wide area communications products," Dusa said.
Research firms have estimated that the remote access market could be valued at US$8-12 billion in the year 2000 from about US$4 billion currently, Dusa said.
Remote access was about 25 percent of Digi's business now with its multi-user single computer business at 50 percent.
Dusa said its multi-user business was slowing. But strong growth was seen in remote access and its subsidiary MiLAN Technology, which deals in products used in the physical layer of a network.
Digi was controlling its shipments to distributors and saw inventory reach a "normalcy level" - the inventory period desired by its distributors - by its fourth quarter.
The company was negotiating to sell its business acquired from a company called LAN Access and some other products that duplicated what it already had.
Digi was continuing to look at new products and companies and would make more acquisitions if it was in line with its strategy, but it would not be for diversification, Dusa said.

Its cash level had improved to US$15 million from US$5.0 million at the beginning of its second quarter, sufficient for its operations, he said. Digi had no plans to raise additional capital, he added.
On his visit to Asia, Dusa said he came to find out how Digi could make investments to boost the contribution from the region which was presently at 10 percent. But there were no plans yet, he added.
-- Singapore newsroom (65-8703080)
